sentences.text: Vola was eleven and lived, most of the year, in a small apartment in Antananarivo — the capital of Madagascar, which everyone she knew called Tana.
Her mother worked in a bank.
Her father was a schoolteacher.
Vola went to a good school and spoke French and Malagasy and was learning English.
She had lived her whole life in the city.
Every year in July, when it was winter in the highlands — dry and cool and quiet — Vola took the long bus ride south to her grandmother's village.
The village was called Ambohimena, and it sat in a small green valley about six hours from Tana by taxi-brousse.
Her grandmother, whom Vola called Bebe, lived there alone in a small red-earth house with a thatched roof.
Bebe was sixty-eight.
She had lived in the same house her entire adult life.
And she was, though Vola had not really understood this before, one of the last people in her region who really knew how to weave the old lamba.
Vola arrived at the house on the first afternoon of July.
Bebe was standing in the doorway, one hand up to shade her eyes.
She had known which taxi Vola would come on because she knew the schedule the way she knew the tides.
When Vola climbed the last of the path with her small backpack, Bebe smiled a wide slow smile and said, "You are taller.
Come.
There is soup."
Inside, the house was one large room and a small side room with a bed.

The main room had a small stove, a table, two chairs, a low shelf of cooking pots, and, along the whole of one wall, a stack of woven lamba — the long rectangular cloths that Malagasy people wore wrapped around their bodies, or draped over their shoulders, or given as gifts, or, when someone died, wrapped around them for burial.
The stack was neat and tall.
Bebe had woven every one of them.
In the yard outside, under a shelter of woven raffia mats stretched over four wooden posts, was Bebe's loom.
It was very big — as wide as Vola was tall, and about half as long again — and made of dark wood polished by generations of hands.
A partly-finished cloth was stretched across it, held taut by weights of small round stones.
The colors were red-brown, deep purple, and cream, with a black line every so often.
Vola had seen Bebe at the loom before, but she had never been old enough to sit at it and try.
"This year," Bebe said, over the soup, "we will make you a lamba.
Your first.
You will start it, you will finish it, and you will take it home to your mother.
Not fancy.
A simple one.
But yours.
That is what this July is for." Vola was very pleased.
She had wanted this for two years.
The first week, they only did the simple things.
Bebe showed Vola how to sit at the loom — legs crossed, back straight but relaxed, weight settled.
She showed Vola how to hold the shuttle.
She showed her the motion of passing it through the warp threads, and pressing down the beater to lock each row of weft in place.
She did not let Vola do very much at first.
"Watch," she kept saying.
"Watch first.
Weaving is not something the hands learn.
It is something the eyes learn.
The hands only follow."
So Vola watched.
Bebe worked on the piece already in the loom — a red-brown wrap with cream borders — and Vola sat beside her and watched every movement.
By the end of the week, Vola could see what Bebe was doing even before she did it.
Her hands began to want to move.
Bebe smiled and said, "Now.
Now the hands know.
This is the moment.
Sit."
That evening, after they had eaten and cleaned the plates, Bebe took Vola over to the wall of stacked lamba.
From very near the bottom of the stack, she pulled out a very old one, folded small.
She carried it to the table and laid it out.
It was long — nearly as long as the table — and pale cream, with a dense pattern of small red-brown geometric shapes running across it.
The shapes were not repeating in the usual way.
They were arranged in an order Vola could not quite see.
"This one was my grandmother's," Bebe said.
"Her name was Ravaka.
She wove it before I was born.
It came to me when my mother died.
My mother told me, once, that this lamba was different from the ones Ravaka made for selling.
She said Ravaka wove it for the family.
She said, this one carries something.
And I would tell you what, my mother said, but Ravaka never told me.
She only told me it was here." Bebe touched the pattern lightly with two fingers.
"My mother said, if you ever understand it, you understand it.
But she never did.
And I never have.
Sixty years I have looked at this pattern.
I cannot read it.
Something is here.
I don't know what." She folded it again and put it away.
"Sleep," she said.
"Tomorrow, more weaving."
